![Thumbnail for Jeff Dean's Princeton CS Distinguished Colloquium of February 10, 2026. [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0)](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Jeff Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Dean), Chief Scientist for [Google Research](https://research.google/) and [Google DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/) and a co-lead of [Gemini](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini/), gave the [Princeton CS](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/) Distinguished Colloquium on February 10, 2026. His title was "Important Trends in AI: How Did We Get Here, What Can We Do Now, and Where are We Headed?" The talk runs 78 minutes. About 40 of them are a chronological tour of the advances that produced current models, most of which he either worked on or sat next to. The rest is Gemini, the logistics of a thousand-author project, and four audience questions.

Six months after this talk, on August 5, 2026, [Dean announced he was leaving Google](https://www.wired.com/story/jeff-dean-google-discovery-loop-startup/) after almost 27 years. He is now CEO of Discovery Loop, a public benefit corporation set up to automate the scientific method itself across chip design, biology, drug discovery, and material design. Three colleagues left with him: [Sanjay Ghemawat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Ghemawat), his collaborator on much of Google's core infrastructure, plus [Oriol Vinyals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriol_Vinyals) and [Quoc Le](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quoc_V._Le), two of the three researchers he credits by name in this lecture for the sequence-to-sequence work. Google took a stake and agreed to supply compute for the first year.

The talk, in brief:

- **[Scale and architecture multiply rather than add](#ch-four-observations).** His summary of the last 13 or 14 years: 20× from scale times 50× from better architectures is a thousand-fold improvement, and both terms have kept delivering.
- **[His 1990 undergraduate thesis was model-parallel and data-parallel training](#h-thesis)**, under the names "pattern partitioned" and "pipelined." The speedup curves tapered off because he held the model size fixed while adding processors, and he then left the subject alone for 25 years.
- **[The TPU program started from one back-of-envelope calculation](#h-tpu-origin)**: a billion users talking to a good speech model three minutes a day would have required doubling the number of computers Google had.
- **[Silent data corruption is treated as a first-class training problem](#h-sdc)**, with per-layer gradient-norm monitoring, automatically triggered deterministic replay to separate bad hardware from bad batches, and hot spares swapped into a synchronous job mid-run.
- **[Gemini's IMO gold medal came with more specialization than the talk describes](#h-imo).** It solved five of six problems. The public record adds reinforcement-learning training on multi-step reasoning data, a corpus of high-quality solutions, and IMO-specific instructions, while the talk describes an out-of-the-box model given a large thinking budget.
- **[Inference efficiency is where he expects the next gains](#ch-forward-looking)**, along with attending to a trillion tokens through learned retrieval instead of a larger context window.
- **[Slope beats absolute score](#h-small-scale)** in his answer to an audience member who asked what to do with a thousand TPUs. Run the same idea at three tiny sizes and read the trend: an idea below the baseline with a good slope is more interesting than one that starts above it and decays.

The video has no chapter markers, so the **[enriched transcript](#transcript) at the bottom of this post** has its own outline: 11 sections and 61 topic subsections, each section linking to its YouTube timestamp. It also adds hyperlinks on first mention, bracketed acronym expansions, and editor's notes on the handful of claims worth checking. The outline is in the right-hand sidebar.

Dean presents slides throughout, and the audio alone does not always say what is on them. 65 slides are captured below, each placed near the point in the transcript where he speaks to it and captioned with a link to that moment in the video. The Q&A has none, since the camera stays on the room.

### [0:00:12 — Introduction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=12s) {#ch-introduction}

**Kai Li:** Good afternoon. It's not 4:30 yet, but since the room is already full, I'll just start doing introduction to save some time. Okay. It's a real pleasure to introduce Jeff Dean, a chief scientist for Google Research and the Google DeepMind, and also he's a co-lead of Gemini project.

I would say before the now famous Jeff Dean at Google era, I actually met Jeff in the 90s when Jeff was in [Digital Western Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Equipment_Corporation), and so I can confirm is not overnight success story. *Jeff has been quietly exceptional for a very long time.*

Jeff's bio you probably read in the flyer reads a little bit like a guided tour of modern computing, from large-scale information retrieval, operating system, distributed system, compilers. And then if that wasn't enough, the second career is that AI machine, you know, ML accelerator, vision model, low-level software — I'm going to not upgrade Chrome right now [laughter] — and also distillation, neural network architecture search, large language multimodal model, and application ranging from chip design to healthcare, translation, and so on.

So one of my favorite details of Jeff is that he did his undergraduate thesis on neural networks, and which means two things I think. First, he worked on neural network before it was cool. And second, he has the rare distinction being able to say I like neural network before Google made it popular. Okay, maybe Jeff did that to himself.

But if you're wondering what takes to be good, to have a good research taste, apparently the answer is start early to be Jeff. So along the way Jeff has received the [ACM Prize in Computing](https://awards.acm.org/acm-prize), [IEEE John von Neumann] Medal. He's a [ACM fellow](https://awards.acm.org/fellows), a member of US [National Academy of Engineering](https://www.nae.edu/) and [American Academy of Arts and Sciences](https://www.amacad.org/).

### [0:02:56 — Four observations about where AI is](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=176s) {#ch-four-observations}

**Kai Li:** So, we're very fortunate to have him to give us the distinguished lecture today. Please join me to welcome Jeff.

**Jeff Dean:** All right. [applause] Thank you very much for that kind introduction and for hosting me. I'm unexpectedly in town and Kai said, "Hey, you want to come by and give a talk?" So, I'm delighted to be here.

And I'm going to talk to you about what's happening in AI. I don't know if you've noticed, but it's a thing these days. And we have many people at Google working on this area. So, I'm presenting the work of not just my work, but many, many people at Google and elsewhere.

#### Computers can now see, hear, and read

So, a few observations which may not come as a huge surprise to you. So machine learning and AI have really changed our expectations of what is possible with computers. You know, if you think back 10, 15 years ago, computers couldn't see very well. They couldn't really understand speech all that well. They definitely couldn't understand language very well.

![The four observations the talk opens with. Slide at [0:03:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=227s).](slide-012.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And now we have tools that enable computers to interact with people in a much more natural style because they understand the modalities that people understand and want to communicate with.

#### Scale times algorithms: 20× and 50× make 1000×

And along the way, increasing scale of larger amounts of compute, larger amounts of data, and more larger scale models have delivered better results nearly continuously for the last sort of 13 or 14 years. This has been the trend and seems to be holding up even today.

In addition to scale, algorithmic and sort of model architecture improvements have also provided massive improvements as well. And *these two things multiply together*, right? If you can have much larger scale and much better model architectures that are able to learn more per floating point operation, those things together mean instead of 20x from scale, you have 20x from scale and 50x from algorithms and you end up with a thousandx better thing than you had not that long ago.

### [0:05:00 — Neural nets, backpropagation, and a 1990 undergraduate thesis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=300s) {#ch-early-thesis}

Also, the kinds of computations we want to run and the hardware in which we want to run them are changing dramatically.

So four observations which are maybe not surprising. First, neural nets and [gradient descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent). These seem to be key building blocks for how do you actually build truly intelligent computer systems.

![Section title. Slide at [0:05:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=313s).](slide-013.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Not new ideas: the 70s, the 80s, and an intro lecture in 1990

And they're not new ideas. They're things that have been around for a long time. They were invented in the 70s and 80s. And there was actually a lot of excitement about them in the late 80s and early 90s.

I first ran across them in an intro lecture where I was introduced to [neural networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network_(machine_learning)) roughly like this. You know, we have this kind of nice very abstracted away version of how we think real life neurons behave, where you have a bunch of inputs, you do some processing, and you decide are you going to fire or not, and what strength are you going to fire, and you have connections of these things.

And then [back propagation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation) is a really nice algorithm that enables you to adjust the weights on the edges of all these connections in order to make the model behave more in the way that you want it to behave, where you give it a bunch of examples and back propagation enables you to make the model learn the behavior you want.

![Backpropagation as the second key building block, with the gradient-descent plots beside it. Slide at [0:06:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=361s).](slide-014.jpg){fig-align="center"}

So I saw these as an undergrad in 1990 and I got super excited and I said, "Oh wow, that seems like a really good abstraction. It feels like it's a trainable thing and it can learn almost anything."

#### A senior thesis that was model parallelism and data parallelism {#h-thesis}

And at that time we were not using very large neural networks because we had really pathetically wimpy computers. But I said, "Oh, maybe if we use the parallel computer in the department, we could train much bigger neural networks. That would be great. Maybe we just need to use 32 computers instead of one and then we could train really impressive neural nets. That would be nice."

So, I did it. I asked the professor who introduced the neural networks topic in one of the classes I was taking if I could do a senior thesis with him, [Vipin Kumar](https://cse.umn.edu/cs/vipin-kumar). And he said, "Sure."

So I played around with two different approaches for training neural networks in parallel. One is *this is what you would now call model parallel and data parallel training*. But I called them pattern partitioned and pipelined approach.

And these speed up curves are interesting but they taper off because I did the stupid thing. I didn't make the model bigger and bigger as I increase the number of processors. I just made it much harder to parallelize with a fixed size model.

![The 1990 senior thesis and its Fig. 2, where both parallel approaches flatten away from the dotted linear-speedup line as processors are added. The network was three layers of 10, 21, and 10 neurons. Slide at [0:07:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=460s).](thesis-1990.jpg){fig-align="center"}

But I sort of filed that away as like, oh, that's an interesting abstraction and it seems like something I should pay attention to. But then I ignored it for the next 25 years.

![Section title for the 15-year tour. Slide at [0:07:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=475s).](slide-016.jpg){fig-align="center"}

### [0:08:00 — Scaling up: DistBelief, word2vec, seq2seq, and the first TPUs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=480s) {#ch-scaling-up}

Okay. So now I'm going to give you a whirlwind tour of a bunch of advances in the field of ML that have happened in the last 15 years that are really all combined together to produce today's most sophisticated models. How did these today's models come to be? Well, it was through advancements like the ones I'm going to describe.

![DistBelief: model parallelism across a network, data parallelism across replicas, and the parameter servers between them. Slide at [0:08:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=504s).](slide-017.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Bumping into Andrew Ng in a micro kitchen

So, the origin of my getting back to working on neural nets at Google was I bumped into [Andrew Ng](https://www.andrewng.org/), who's a Stanford faculty member, in one of our micro kitchens and I said, "Oh, what are you doing here?" He's like, "I'm not sure yet, because I just started a week ago. But my students at Stanford are doing interesting things with training neural networks for speech and vision."

I'm like, "Oh, that's cool. We should train really big neural networks," because we actually had quite a lot of computers in those days. And I said, "Oh, why don't we try training very, very large neural networks?"

#### Asynchronous replicas and parameter servers: "theoretically wrong" but it worked

And so we built [a software system](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/hash/6aca97005c68f1206823815f66102863-Abstract.html) [[1]](#ref-1) that enabled us to express neural network and connectivity of those neural networks and do both model and data parallel training across many, many computers. And that enabled us to train neural networks that were *50 to 100 times larger* than the largest ones we could find anyone talking about.

And we had a way of doing this where we had actually many, many asynchronous replicas of the model getting updates of what the current parameters of the model were, churning away on their local batch of examples, computing a gradient and sending it to this distributed set of parameter servers in order to update the parameters of the model.

This is, because it's asynchronous, definitely not the right mathematical thing, because in the meantime the model parameters have moved from the other replicas giving the parameter servers updates to the parameters. But it seemed to work, so we were sort of happy anyway despite it being sort of theoretically wrong.

#### Cat neurons from 10 million unlabeled YouTube frames

And one of the first things we trained was a very large model to do [completely unsupervised learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209) [[2]](#ref-2) on 10 million random YouTube frames. And interestingly, we had a kind of a locally connected neural network for computer vision that would use a reconstruction loss.

So we try to take a high level representation of the neurons at the highest level of the model and then try to reconstruct the pixels that have been given as input, and because that bottleneck layer forced the model to sort of learn higher level abstractions than the actual raw pixels.

What we ended up finding was at the top level of this model, *some of the neurons had learned to be sensitive to whether or not there was a face of a cat in the image*. Some of them learned to be sensitive to whether there was a face. Some were sensitive to, you know, is this the outline of a person. All without being told any of these images contained any of those kinds of objects. So it's kind of neat to see that you could learn these high level abstractions and representations from a purely unsupervised objective.

#### A 70% relative improvement on ImageNet 22k

What we could then do is use the initialization of this unsupervised training in order to train with a supervised method to try to do computer vision image classification. And we used, unfortunately we used, the 22,000 category version of [ImageNet](https://www.image-net.org/), which is a more thinly traded version than the 1000 category one that most people are most familiar with.

![The cat neuron, and the ImageNet 22K table showing 15.8% with unsupervised pretraining against a 9.3% state of the art. Slide at [0:11:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=698s).](slide-018.jpg){fig-align="center"}

But we got a 70% relative improvement in ImageNet 22k state-of-the-art by initializing with our unsupervised model and then doing supervised learning on the training set for that data set, which is quite a large relative improvement. So we were happy with that and we saw that scale really mattered.

![word2vec, with the king/queen and walking/walked direction examples. Slide at [0:12:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=747s).](slide-019.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### word2vec: nearby words cluster, and directions mean something

We also started to do a bunch of work in using neural networks for language tasks. And one of the things we found was that even relatively simple models where you have [a vector-based representation of words or phrases](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781) [[3]](#ref-3), so that you have a nice thousand or 500 dimensional representation of each word or token, and have relatively shallow models.

So in fact we had just the embedding vector, and then we would use the embedding vector of the word to try to predict nearby words. That was one of the approaches we tried.

And what we found was that if you apply this to lots of text and use this training objective, you end up with nearby words in the high-dimensional space tend to be related ones. So like cat and puma and tiger are all low distance in the high-dimensional space. And also that *directions are meaningful*. So you go in the same direction to change the gender of a word in a gendered language regardless of what word you start with. King and queen.

![Sequence to sequence learning, with the encoder state initializing the decoder. Slide at [0:13:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=823s).](slide-020.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### seq2seq: an LSTM encoder's final state as the decoder's initial state

A year or two later, three of my colleagues [Ilya Sutskever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilya_Sutskever), [Oriol Vinyals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriol_Vinyals) and [Quoc Le](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quoc_V._Le) [used a neural encoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) [[4]](#ref-4) using an [LSTM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_short-term_memory) [long short-term memory] to essentially be able to learn an encoder for one sequence and then a decoder for a different sequence.

And when you initialize the state of the LSTM by running the encoder, that ends up sort of capturing the things that have occurred in that input sequence and enables the model to then use that initial state to then do a good job of predicting the target sequence.

So the canonical example use case of this is language translation, where maybe you have a bunch of English-French sentence pairs that mean the same thing and the input sentence is English. And so when you're training you try to decode the French sentence and you get a supervised learning objective for every token or for every word. And then when you're trying to translate a new sentence you just use the encoder to encode the LSTM state and then decode from that state in order to produce the translated French.

#### The back-of-envelope calculation that started the TPU program {#h-tpu-origin}

So as we saw more and more success of neural networks, and in particular scaling up neural networks for problems in computer vision, speech recognition and language, we were starting to both get excited but also a bit worried about how we would actually deploy these much better models.

So this is kind of the origin of how we started to create our own [tensor processing unit](https://cloud.google.com/tpu) chip program. I did this back of the envelope calculation and said, okay, we have this really nice high quality speech recognition model. It has the error rate for speech recognition which is a huge improvement. It's sort of equivalent to *20 years of speech research in like six months* since we started the project, by training just a very large, not particularly sophisticated model architecture. It's like an eight layer fully connected neural net just trained on a lot of data.

![The back-of-envelope slide itself, from an internal infrastructure review in May 2013: a billion users at three minutes of speech a day works out to roughly 20 million core days per day. Slide at [0:15:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=902s).](slide-021.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And that back of the envelope calculation said *if we wanted to deploy this to a scenario where we had a billion users talking to this model 3 minutes a day, we would need to double the number of computers Google had*. And that didn't seem very tenable for rolling out a better speech recognition system.

So that really convinced us that exploring much more specialized computational devices for doing neural network inference and later neural network training was going to be a fruitful path. And so this sort of bootstrap got us to really approach that with conviction and started up a chip design team in order to build these chips.

#### TPUv1: reduced precision and a handful of linear-algebra operations

And then the first chip emerged two years later, as hardware projects tend to do. They take a little while, but we eventually produced [the TPUv1 chip](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.04760) [[5]](#ref-5), which took advantage of two really nice properties of neural networks.

![TPUv1 at 92 teraops, inference only, exploiting reduced precision and a handful of linear-algebra operations. Slide at [0:16:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1009s).](slide-022.jpg){fig-align="center"}

The first is that reduced precision is fine, especially for inference. So you're perfectly happy with about seven or eight bits of precision, not 16 or 32 or 64 as most people are thinking about in terms of floating-point computation things.

And also that nearly all of the models we were exploring were made up of different combinations of a handful of specific kinds of linear algebra operations. You know, things like matrix multiplies are at the heart of them, and then certain kinds of dot products and normalization and scaling.

But if you think about most of the machine learning algorithms of today, different rearrangements of those kinds of operations mean that you can build an accelerator that is capable of very high performance reduced precision linear algebra and that can be applicable to a pretty wide range of neural networks. And it's much more efficient because that's all it needs to do. It doesn't need to do anything else. *It doesn't need to run Microsoft Word or Chrome or anything else.*

And so TPUv1 turned out to be 15 to 30x faster than contemporary CPUs and GPUs and 30 to 80 times more energy efficient than contemporary CPUs and GPUs. And it's also now the most cited paper in [ISCA](https://www.iscaconf.org/)'s [International Symposium on Computer Architecture] 50-year history.

![TPU pods: thousands of chips on a custom high-speed network. Slide at [0:18:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1115s).](slide-023.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Optical interconnect and racks you can swap mid-run

So we then turned the chip design team's attention to the training problem, because we felt like being able to scale up training more than we were able to on CPUs and GPUs was going to be important. And so this is where the focus has been for quite a while.

And we've now produced many, many generations of TPUs that are essentially machine learning supercomputers, right? It's more than just a single chip, unlike TPUv1. Instead it's lots and lots of chips connected with a custom high-speed interconnect that enables us to distribute model training over those chips and communicate both activations and parameter updates and gradient updates across that custom interconnect.

Version four introduced this funky thing where we have an optical interconnect for racks of these accelerators. So, there's a rack of 64 accelerators and *we can make it seem as though that rack of 64 accelerators is right next to another rack of 64 accelerators even though they're 100 meters across the data center floor*.

And if that rack fails, we can swap in another rack and make it seem as though this rack is now right next to that one in terms of the net topology. Which is important. As you get more and more scale, you end up with failures. And so you want to be able to reconfigure things like that.

#### Reading the generation table: TPUv4 to Ironwood

And so we've seen continual hardware performance scaling. So if you look at TPUv4 here on the left column, the peak flops per chip is about 275 teraflops. The max pod size was 4,896 chips, and now we're sort of at roughly double that pod size and much, much more [HBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory) [high-bandwidth memory] and much more memory bandwidth and many more flops per chip.

![The table Dean reads from: TPU v4 (2022), v5p (2023), and Ironwood (2025) at 4,896 / 8,960 / 9,216 chips per pod and 275 / 459 / 4,614 TFLOPS per chip, with Ironwood's pod at ~3600× TPU v2. Slide at [0:20:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1215s).](tpu-generations.jpg){fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** Two things about that table. Ironwood is Google's *seventh*-generation TPU: the sixth is [Trillium](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/introducing-trillium-sixth-generation-tpu), announced at Google I/O in May 2024 and generally available that December, and it is the generation the table skips, going v5p straight to Ironwood. Dean flags the numbering as confusing in the same breath, since Google dropped the "v7" branding for Ironwood. Separately, the TPU v4 pod size shown as 4,896 is [documented by Google as 4,096 chips](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/v4), and the [TPU v4 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01433) cited on Dean's own earlier slide also gives 4,096. The transcript reproduces the figure he read off the slide.
:::

If you compare the peak performance per pod, which is sort of the largest network configuration we have of the custom interconnect, the TPUv2 pod is 1x and the most recent sort of v6 — but now we've stopped numbering them, sadly, it's harder to keep track of, but [Ironwood](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/ironwood-tpus-generally-available) is the sixth generation of TPUs — is about 3600 times the performance per pod of TPUv2. And it's also much more energy efficient, so about 30x better flops per watt, which is what you ultimately care about.

![The same scaling in energy terms, roughly 30x better flops per watt than TPU v2. Slide at [0:21:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1263s).](slide-025.jpg){fig-align="center"}

![TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX. Slide at [0:21:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1279s).](slide-026.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX

The other thing that has happened in the last 15 years is open source tools have really enabled the whole community to build using the same pieces of abstraction and software libraries, and the community can work on sort of improving those tools as well.

So we developed a software called [TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/) based on our initial lessons from the sort of 2011 to 2014 era with an internal software library that we were using to parallelize computations across many computers and train large models and do inference.

And then more recently various people at [Meta](https://about.meta.com/) and elsewhere introduced [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/), and then another group of people at Google have introduced a more functional style paradigm computation called [JAX](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax). All of these are great systems, and we have been using JAX for our Gemini training and it's been great.

### [0:22:30 — Transformers, sparsity, and the training substrate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1350s) {#ch-transformers-sparsity}

#### Why LSTMs don't parallelize: one state update per token

And then in 2017 a number of my colleagues worked on [coming up with a better architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) [[6]](#ref-6) than the sort of recurrent LSTMs that were kind of the state-of-the-art models for language at the time.

And the observation they had was really, in an LSTM you have a vector of state of sort of the current representation of the state, and then when you advance one token at a time you update that state, and there's a sophisticated thing that updates the state, and then you go on to the next word and you update the state again. And so as you progress through say a hundred words of a sentence you update the state a 100 times.

And there's two problems with that. One is you have this sequential process. Every word you have to wait for the update of the state, and there's a sequential dependency on that state being ready before you can go on to update the state for the next word. So, it's not very parallelizable, which is not good on modern hardware.

And the other thing is you're trying to force all the things you went through into a single vector, that you have all the things you might want to remember from the things you went through in a single vector, rather than just saving all the vectors you went through and then being able to look at them as you wish later in the sort of language modeling process.

#### Save the vectors and learn where to look

So the key observation in the transformer model is *let's save all those vectors, or some representation of those vectors, and then pay attention to them in a way where we have a learnable attention mechanism*.

![Test loss against parameter count, with the Transformer curves below the one, two, and four-layer LSTMs at every scale. Slide at [0:24:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1449s).](slide-027.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And what they were able to show was that compared to LSTMs of one, two or four layers in red there, the test loss on the y-axis went down considerably using a transformer, and no matter what model scale you looked at. So sort of *10 to 100x less compute and 10 times smaller model* gave you with a transformer roughly the same quality as you would get with an LSTM that's much larger.

#### Self-supervised learning: there is a lot of text in the world

In 2018, I think people really started to take seriously the idea, well, I guess in the word2vec work we were already sort of doing that, but in 2018, really looking at how could you do language modeling at scale with self-supervised data. And just the observation there's a lot of text in the world.

And so self-supervised learning on this text can give you almost unlimited amounts of training data where you know the right answer, right? Like you have text and then you hide the next word and you try to guess the next word, and if you guess it correctly that gives you a sort of a one, and if you guess it wrong that gives you a clear error signal that you can propagate into improving the model, so that in such settings you will guess better next time. And so this is really one of the major reasons that these chat and language models have gotten so good.

#### Autoregressive against fill-in-the-blank

And so there are two kinds of training objectives that people typically use. One is called autoregressive, where you get to look at the prefix, everything to the left, and try to predict the next word. So "Princeton blank," you know, that word is a little bit hard to predict. Could be Princeton New Jersey, could be Princeton University. "Princeton University blank." That one's hard to predict as well. "Is cold in the blank," that one's a little easier to predict. So that's autoregressive.

![The two self-supervised objectives, worked on "Princeton University is cold in the ___" for autoregressive and on a masked sentence for fill-in-the-blank. Slide at [0:26:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1576s).](slide-028.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And then [fill in the blank](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) [[7]](#ref-7) is where you get to have a training objective where you just hide, you get to look in both directions and you hide some of the words and you try to force the model to guess the missing words that you've hidden. And again, you get this nice sophisticated, you know, very, very crisp error signal that you can use to train the model. And you can just train on lots and lots of text, either of the objectives.

The fill-in-the-blank one tends to be used to build representations that give you a good representation of a bunch of text, but you can't really use it for a chatbot because you don't have the things to the right. So you have to sort of end up using mostly autoregressive models for conversational applications, but fill-in-the-blank also has some good uses.

#### Vision Transformers against ResNet-152

In 2021 a number of other of my colleagues [applied transformers to computer vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929) [[8]](#ref-8). At that time the sort of state-of-the-art was to use various kinds of convolutional models, which have these kind of local receptive fields, and then you build up and share the parameters among different positions in the image. And instead you can just apply a transformer based model to the same problem.

And what they found was again you get a much better, you know, if you look at the TPU core days to reach certain levels of accuracy, the TPU core days are much lower and the accuracy is higher compared with say [ResNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) [[9]](#ref-9) 152, which was kind of a good state-of-the-art model at the time.

![Vision Transformers, with what the attention mechanism looks at and the benchmark table against ResNet and EfficientNet. Slide at [0:28:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1680s).](slide-029.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And the other nice thing is you can kind of see what the attention mechanism is paying attention to. So it gives you a little bit of model interpretation of like what is it paying attention to in order to make a say a classification prediction that that middle one is an airplane.

#### Sparse models: the part that thinks about Shakespeare stays off

Another area that we have done a bunch of work in, including myself, is in [sparse models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538) [[10]](#ref-10). In a dense model you have a bunch of parameters in the model and every inference or every token you activate the entire model in order to make the prediction for that example.

![The sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer, and the perplexity-against-compute chart the A-or-B choice is read off: (A) about 8x less training compute for the same accuracy, or (B) a better model for the same compute. The slide credits Shazeer et al., ICLR 2017 [[10]](#ref-10). Slide at [0:28:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1694s).](slide-030.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And that seems kind of, that's not how our brains work, right? We have very different pieces of our brains that are useful for different kinds of things. And we activate the right part. So *while I'm worried about the garbage truck backing up at my car, some parts of my brain are active and the part that thinks about Shakespearean poetry is not active*.

So with sparse models the idea is we want to have different pieces of the model that are good at different kinds of things, and then be able to automatically learn not just those experts but also learn the routing mechanism to learn which pieces of the model to actually activate for those different examples.

#### Choice A or choice B: 8× less training compute, or a better model

And so it gives the model much larger capacity but still keeps the inference cost relatively low, because you're only activating a small number of the parameters in the model. And importantly, it gives you an 8x reduction in training compute for the same accuracy. That's choice A there.

Or you could choose to spend the same amount on training the model and get a much better model, right? Same amount of compute. That would be choice B there. And often these kinds of things you choose a bit of A and B and end up kind of somewhere there.

But this has been a really important tool for making our model better and better over time, is having [sparsity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) [[11]](#ref-11) be part of the mix. There's a whole litany of work that both I and my colleagues have done in this general area looking at various aspects of how to do the routing, you know, how many experts do you have.

![The sparse-model bibliography, from Shazeer 2017 through DiPaCo in 2024. Slide at [0:29:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1799s).](slide-031.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Pathways: one Python process driving tens of thousands of chips

Another thing we've been working on is building up abstractions for distributed ML computations. So [Pathways](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.12533) [[12]](#ref-12) is a system we started working on quite a while ago that really wants to abstract away this pile of accelerators underneath your computation and *give the researcher the illusion that you just have a giant computer with tens of thousands of chips attached to it*, and you can mostly just focus on the machine learning computations you're trying to express.

And underneath the covers, Pathways does a bunch of work to manage how to communicate the machine learning computation you've expressed amongst all these chips. And so it will, for example, use within one of these pods, it will use the custom TPU interconnect. When you go across the pod boundary in the same data center building, it will use the data center network. When you go across buildings in the same data center campus, it will use the purple network link. And when you go across perhaps widely distributed metro regions, it will use the sort of wide area network links.

![Pathways spanning buildings and regions, with the whole training process driven from one Python process. Slide at [0:31:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1891s).](slide-032.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And then when you actually put JAX on top of Pathways, what that means is that we can drive the entire training process from a single Python process on one host. So that Python process says, "Oh great, I have access to these many thousands of TPU chips," and I can run this computation, and Pathways kind of deals with what happens when different pieces of the system fail and swapping in new parts, new hardware under the covers.

![Silent data corruption introduced, alongside the "Cores that don't count" paper. Slide at [0:32:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1923s).](slide-033.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Silent data corruption, sometimes temperature-dependent {#h-sdc}

Another thing that tends to happen when you run at increasingly large scale is sadly not all chips or machines or network cards or cables work as designed. That's a very sad but true state of the world.

And in particular, some of them don't just fail in ways that you can just like detect them immediately and replace them. They sometimes non-deterministically sort of produce incorrect results silently, and sometimes that's related to dynamic conditions like *the temperature of the rack at that particular moment*.

This is really challenging when you're running independent compute on these things, but it's really worse when you're trying to have all these chips perform as a single orchestrated machine learning training computation where everything is synchronous, and this can quickly spread bad results. So like if one of these things flips one of the bits in the exponent field of your gradient, all of a sudden you'll get 10 to the 20th propagating as a gradient instead of 0.2, and that makes you very, very sad.

![A gradient-norm spike that was caused by silent data corruption. Slide at [0:33:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=1998s).](slide-034.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Gradient-norm spikes, and replaying a step to find out why

And so we monitor during the training process all kinds of metrics about the health of our model. And in particular, you can look at, for example, the norm of the gradient at every layer of the model and see are you seeing spikes in that. So here's an example of a spike due to one of these silent data corruption things.

Now not all spikes are necessarily due to these kinds of machine issues. Here's another spike. There is no SDC. This is just some particular batch of examples that contain something that caused a very large gradient to occur. And it's a little hard to discern those things.

![A gradient-norm anomaly with no silent data corruption behind it, which is the case that makes the two hard to tell apart. Slide at [0:33:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2025s).](sdc-anomaly.jpg){fig-align="center"}

So one of the ways we do this is *we have deterministic replay that we trigger automatically*. So if we see a gradient spike, then we will effectively replay that step or the last few steps and see if we get the same answer. And if we get the same answer, we conclude, well, that's probably okay. That was probably due to the data, not due to hardware errors. But if the hardware errors are causing the issue, then hopefully we get a different answer the next time.

![The opposite failure: corruption detected by replay while the gradient norm stayed in its normal range. Slide at [0:34:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2073s).](slide-038.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And you can also have cases where we don't get a gradient spike but there is actually silent data corruption happening, but it doesn't cause a very large spike in the gradient, and so that is sort of benign to the model even though we didn't detect it. So all kinds of things can happen. It's very fun.

![How Pathways handles it, with an SDC checker on the idle chips and a hot spare swapped in for the defective machine. Slide at [0:34:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2096s).](slide-039.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Hot spares, and an SDC checker running on the idle chips

The Pathways system is part of the way in which we transparently handle these things. So for example, let's say these blue pods or slices of pods are currently part of our synchronous training jobs. We have these seven blue things. We have a hot spare in gray, and then we have another hot spare and we're running an SDC checker. So we have a continuous thing that we're running even on the idle chips in order to try to weed out bad hardware before we're actually starting to use it.

The defective machine causes one of these silent data corruptions. The SDC checker identifies this because we replayed and detected that there was a mismatch in the answers when we ran them twice. And we can pinpoint which pod it is and which chips. We can evict that thing and then use the hot spare to now replace it transparently in the training process and continue on our merry way. Send that thing to our repairs team and hopefully they can figure out in more detail what's going on.

### [0:36:15 — Chain of thought, distillation, RL, and speculative decoding](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2175s) {#ch-inference-techniques}

#### Chain of thought: what your fourth grade math teacher told you

Okay. In 2022, thinking longer at inference time became more of a thing. And in particular the observation was that [if you prompt the model to show more of its work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903) [[13]](#ref-13) on an example problem and then ask it to solve a similar kind of problem.

You know, if you just asked the answer, please give me the answer, in this example you prompted the model with one example problem and you said the answer is nine. And then you gave it the problem you really care about, and the model will sort of model that behavior and say that the answer is 50, and it actually gets this problem wrong.

But if you give the model a worked out example, then the model will tend to work out in the same similar way the individual steps to get through the actual problem solving process and be more likely to give you the correct answer, right? Which is kind of nice. *This is what your fourth grade math teacher told you, and it's nice to see that ML models behave the same way.*

#### Every token is a pass through the model, so answer length is compute

And one way to view this is you're actually giving the model more compute to think at inference time, right? Because every token it needs to generate is a pass through the model. And so you can think of the length of the answer as some proportional aspect of how much compute is devoted to producing the answer.

And what you see is that as the model gets to a certain scale, when you encourage it with chain of thought prompting, you get pretty large increases in the solving rate of [GSM8K](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) [[14]](#ref-14). Remember, this is like eighth grade math problems like the ones here. John has five rabbits. He gets two more. Maybe that's not eighth grade, that should be more like fifth grade or second grade. But anyway, these are pretty simple problems, but we were very excited in 2022 about high rates of accuracy improvements on those kinds of problems. Remember that.

![Standard prompting against chain-of-thought prompting on GSM8K, where the two only separate past roughly 100 billion parameters. The worked examples on the slide are Shawn's toys and John's dogs. The rabbits are Dean's own paraphrase. Slide at [0:38:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2280s).](chain-of-thought.jpg){fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** GSM8K's "8K" counts problems rather than grades: the dataset holds 8,500 grade-school math word problems, per the paper that introduced it [[14]](#ref-14). Dean's on-the-fly correction toward "fifth grade or second grade" is closer than his first pass at "eighth grade."
:::

#### Distillation: a probability distribution beats a single right answer

Another thing we worked on was [distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531) [[15]](#ref-15), where you can effectively use a powerful teacher model to make a smaller and cheaper student model from the more sophisticated predictions that the larger model can make.

And in particular, like if you're doing language modeling, "perform the concerto for blank," right, so the true answer in this case was violin, and that's what your training methodology would use as the signal to give you a supervised learning signal.

But if you have a really good model already, what that teacher model can give you is a probability distribution over the likely next words. So it could be violin, could be piano, could be trumpet. *It's almost certainly not airplane, right? Unless there's new concertos I don't know about.* And so that gives a really rich gradient signal at the very top of the model that gives it much more information than just did you get violin or not, which is what the sort of non-distilled loss would give you.

#### 3% of the training data, nearly the full model's accuracy

And so this enables you to get a lot of the capability of a very large model into a much smaller model, and also to do so with much less data perhaps.

![Distillation, with the concerto example and the speech table where soft targets on 3% of the data reach 57.0% test frame accuracy against the baseline's 44.5%. Slide at [0:39:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2384s).](slide-041.jpg){fig-align="center"}

So in the initial experiments in the paper, we were looking at a speech recognition problem. And so we had a baseline where we used 100% of the training set and got a training frame accuracy of 63.4% and a test frame accuracy of 58.9%.

But if you drop the baseline to use just 3% of the training data, then you overfit on that. So you have 67% training frame accuracy but your test frame accuracy plummets to 44.5%. But if you use the soft targets with distillation you get quite a nice training frame accuracy, actually even better than the baseline on the 100% of the training data, with just 3% of the training data, and *your test frame accuracy is nearly as good as the full model trained on 100% of the data*.

So this is a really key technique for effectively enabling you to morph any shaped model into another shape model, often a larger model into a smaller model. This is for example what we use in Gemini to go from the Pro-scale model into a Flash-scale model.

#### Reinforcement learning to elicit the behaviors you want

And then in the last four or five years I would say [reinforcement learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning) has become much more important in eliciting the desired properties that these models have.

And so given a pre-trained model where you've just exposed it to a whole bunch of training data of text, that model has a bunch of capabilities in it, but often you want to help steer the capabilities of these models a bit.

So in particular, you want to maybe encourage behaviors that you want in the way in which the model responds. You might like a certain style of response. You might like to prefer certain length responses for certain kinds of things. You might want safety properties to be put into the model. So don't engage in these kinds of topics, or say something like this in these scenarios. And you also want to enhance the capabilities by showing the model how to tackle more complex problems.

![Where reinforcement learning gets its reward signal, and the open question about non-verifiable domains. Slide at [0:42:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2528s).](slide-042.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Where the reward signal comes from

And so one of the key questions when you use reinforcement learning is *where does the reward signal come from?* But these do dramatically improve the model capability in a lot of domains. And the reward signals, turns out, can come from lots of different places.

So one is you can use [human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741) [[16]](#ref-16). You know, do you like A or B as an answer for this kind of question, and have humans evaluate that and give a reward. Or is this a good answer for this question? They can say yes or no. Those kinds of things can be very effective at making the model's behavior change pretty dramatically with even relatively few examples.

You can also use reinforcement learning from machine feedback, where you have machine feedback from a different model, so often called a reward model. Maybe you can prompt the reward model saying please say whether you prefer response A or B for question Q, and then you generate two responses from your base model and then you ask the reward model which one do you like better, and that gives you a reward signal.

#### Verifiable domains, and the open question of the rest

You can also do RL in verifiable domains like math or coding, and you can for example generate proofs or solutions to be checked with a theorem prover and give a positive reward when the model produces a correct proof for the problem you're trying to solve. You can generate code for coding things where you now have a reward for does the code even compile? Does the code compile and pass the unit test? You get more reward.

So these really help a lot in both math and coding but also in kind of adjacent areas like more sophisticated reasoning and planning in adjacent domains.

I think there's a nice open research question of *how do you improve the effectiveness of RL in non-verifiable domains, and where do you get interesting reward signals from?* Those are things that I think are pretty open and ripe for lots of cool approaches.

![Speculative decoding's three claims: 2x to 3x faster, no architecture change or retraining, and an identical output distribution. Slide at [0:43:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2639s).](slide-043.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Speculative decoding: decoding from a large model is memory bound

In 2023, a few of my colleagues came up with this really nice method for [making inference faster](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192) [[17]](#ref-17).

One of the problems with the autoregressive decoding is, in order to have the attention mechanism have the state it needs when you're prefilling. So if you have an input of a thousand tokens, that you can do completely in parallel. But now if you're going to try to start generating a response, you generate the first token, and then when you finish generating the first token, you can now look at that token and be able to now generate the next token, because you need the attention state for that previous token in order to actually generate the next token.

![The two observations it rests on, that decoding is memory bound and that some tokens are far easier to predict than the square root of seven. Slide at [0:45:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2705s).](slide-046.jpg){fig-align="center"}

So it's a very sequential process, a little bit like the problem we had with LSTMs where you have this sequential decoding phase. And so speculative decoding is a nice approach, and you change only the decoding algorithm. *You don't have to retrain your model. You have no architecture changes, no retraining, and you're guaranteed to have the identical output distribution.*

Okay. So the observation is decoding from very large transformer models is memory bound. So the hardware can do way more floating-point operations than it can transfer all the weights of your model into the multiplier unit in order to do the single token of decoding you want to be able to do.

#### Some tokens are easy: a drafter plus a parallel check

Observation two is that some tokens are a lot easier to predict than others. So, "can you tell me what the square root of seven is? Sure, the square root of seven is blank." Right? That last token is really, really hard for the model to predict. But a lot of the other ones are very easy for the model to predict. Like after the question mark, it can probably make a prediction of four or five tokens and get some of them correct. In particular, some prefix of them correct.

And so the idea is you have a fast drafter model where you don't need the full sophistication of a much larger model, and you can quickly generate the next say eight tokens and then have the target large model check them in parallel. This effectively gives you a batch size now of, instead of one, a batch size of eight. And *if you accept on average four and a half of those eight tokens, then you've made your compute efficiency much, much better*.

So here's an animation of how this works. If you just try decoding with a large slow model at the top, you're decoding one token at a time. And instead if you have a small model at the bottom that's drafting sequences of four tokens at a time, and then the larger model — I'm going to run that again. Okay. So now watch the bottom thing. The drafter is generating the yellow things, and then the upper model is accepting the prefix of them that is correct according to what it wanted to generate based on its own probability distribution.

![The animation mid-run. The drafter has proposed "is the change in color. The leaves start", and the large model has accepted the green prefix and rejected the orange tail. Slide at [0:46:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2810s).](speculative-decoding.jpg){fig-align="center"}

So this actually helps quite a lot in improving the efficiency of inference in these models.

![The summary matrix, from inference algorithms down to the TPU generations. Slide at [0:47:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2829s).](slide-048.jpg){fig-align="center"}

Okay. So a whole bunch of things have come together in order to actually make these modern models work well. You know, lots of innovations in the inference algorithms, in the training algorithms, model architecture, software.

### [0:47:20 — Gemini](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2840s) {#ch-gemini}

![Section title. Slide at [0:47:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2854s).](slide-049.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### "This is stupid, why don't we all work together"

Okay. So now we get to [Gemini](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini/) [[18]](#ref-18). So the sort of origin of Gemini was we actually had multiple separate groups at Google looking at language models, looking at sort of creating multimodal models of various kinds, and *I sort of said this is stupid, why don't we all work together* and have, instead of fragmenting our compute and our ideas, let's all work together and build a single kind of model that is multimodal that has a lot of compute investment behind a more singular effort.

And that's the sort of origin of the Gemini project. And so we started this in February 2023 with a bunch of collaborators from Google DeepMind, Google Research and the rest of Google. And our goal is really train the world's best multimodal models and use them in all the places we can.

![The Gemini project: started February 2023, with the release timeline through Gemini 3 in November 2025. Slide at [0:48:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2895s).](slide-050.jpg){fig-align="center"}

![Figure 2 from the Gemini report, showing interleaved text, image, audio, and video in one input sequence. Slide at [0:48:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2924s).](slide-051.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And so we've produced in that time a number of different sort of iterations of Gemini generations, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and most recently 3.

#### Multimodal from the start, including non-human modalities

And one of the things we wanted was for the model to be multimodal from the start. In particular, we think it's really important that it deal with language, with audio, with images, and with video, as well as other non-human modalities like, in more recent Gemini versions we've been including some small amounts of say LiDAR data or robotic control data, because *you want to at least expose the model to the idea that these kinds of data exist*.

![Gemini as a list of everything already described in the talk. Slide at [0:49:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=2987s).](slide-052.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And then initially in the early Gemini versions we had an image decoder and a text decoder. More recently we've added audio decoders and video decoders, so that we have a single unified model that can reason over input sequences that are mixes of any of these modalities. So you can give it like an image and some text that describes the image or what you want the model to pay attention to, and maybe you have video and some audio, and you can also produce any of those things as output in an interleaved way if you want.

#### Everything in the talk so far, in one system

And as I said, we're basically building on lots of these different advances. So we use TPUs, we use model parallel and data parallel training and cross data center training. We have fast and automated detection of the SDC errors. We use Pathways, we use JAX, we use distributed representation of words similar to word2vec or the sequence to sequence work.

![Gemini 2.0, announced by Dean. Slide at [0:51:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3084s).](slide-053.jpg){fig-align="center"}

We use transformers. Our models are sparse typically. We distill from larger models into smaller models. We use chain of thought decoding and more sophisticated versions of that. Speculative decoding is really important. We use SFT [supervised fine-tuning] and various kinds of RL, and a bunch of other things I didn't have time to talk about.

#### Long context: crisp input against muddled parameters

One of the things we've been working on for a while is making our [context length](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05530) [[19]](#ref-19) large, because we think the information in the context window for the model is really useful.

You know, unlike tokens in the training data, where you've sort of taken trillions of tokens of training data and stirred them together into hundreds of billions of parameters but it's all a little bit muddled and fuzzy, *the information in the context window of the model, the input that you give it, is very crisp because you haven't mixed it with anything else*.

It's sort of like I see these 900 pages of text you gave me and I can like look at different parts of it and summarize and combine and pull out little pieces of it when I'm decoding. And so extending the context window to very large lengths has been something we've been working on and we think is important.

#### The Pro and Flash ladder: this generation's Flash beats last generation's Pro

One of the things we've tried to keep up with in every release of Gemini since the earliest ones is that we have different scales of models. We have a Pro-scale model which is the highest quality model. And then we have a Flash-scale model that is ideally as close to that Pro-scale model as we can get it.

And in particular, we also want *that Flash-scale model to be better than the previous generation's Pro model*, right? And so we've been able to keep that up for three, four generations now, which we're pretty happy with. Because it means that the highest end thing that is perhaps slower and more expensive for a lot of use cases suddenly becomes more affordable six months from now, because it now has that capability in the Flash-scale model.

Gemini 2.5 Pro we released in March I guess, with quite good results.

![Gemini 2.5 Pro at number one on the Arena leaderboard in March 2025, with what was then the largest score jump. Slide at [0:52:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3136s).](slide-054.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### A gold medal at the IMO {#h-imo}

We've also been working on mathematical problem solving. And in July of last year we competed in the [International Mathematical Olympiad](https://www.imo-official.org/), the IMO, and *we got five out of six problems correct, which is a gold medal score*. We were quite happy with that.

![The IMO result: five of six problems, 35 of 42 points, inside the 4.5-hour limit, quoted from the IMO president. Slide at [0:52:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3146s).](slide-055.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And we did it, we competed the previous year with a more sophisticated kind of jury-rigged mathematically specialized model that used [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/) and theorem provers and various things like that.

For this year we used just an out-of-the-box Gemini Pro-scale model with a high inference thinking time budget in order to tackle these problems. So we were pretty happy that we didn't have the sort of, and we also had in the previous year we had a different model for geometry problems and things like that. So we were happy to have a single general purpose model that is the same one we offered to users was able to solve and get a gold medal at the IMO.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** [Google DeepMind's announcement](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/advanced-version-of-gemini-with-deep-think-officially-achieves-gold-medal-standard-at-the-international-mathematical-olympiad/) describes a more specialized setup than "an out-of-the-box Gemini Pro-scale model with a high inference thinking time budget." The IMO 2025 result came from an advanced version of Gemini Deep Think, a reasoning mode that explores several solution paths in parallel. That Deep Think version was further trained "on novel reinforcement learning techniques that can leverage more multi-step reasoning, problem-solving and theorem-proving data." It was also given access to a corpus of high-quality mathematics solutions and IMO-specific hints in its instructions. The score was 35 of 42 points across five of six problems, inside the 4.5-hour limit. Dean's contrast with the prior year holds: IMO 2024's silver medal came from AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2, which needed problems hand-translated into Lean and took two to three days of computation.
:::

#### Beyond GSM8K: bonza functions

Just to give you a sense of how far we've come in mathematics. Remember back to Fred had five rabbits and then he got two more. Okay, so this is one of the IMO problems. And you can see all the five correct solutions of the problems we did there. But this is one of the problems.

![The bonza-function proof from Problem 3, with the lemma, the construction, and the bound Dean describes. Slide at [0:54:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3253s).](slide-056.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And you can see this is sort of fairly sophisticated mathematical style writing and formatting of proofs and so on. And we established an upper bound. We had another lemma. We constructed and made a lower bound. And then we proved that f of n is less than or equal to 4n for all bonza functions, which was part of the introduction of the problem. So *like this is now quite a bit beyond GSM8K*, I would say. I mean it's not research level mathematics yet, but you can see.

#### Gemini 3, and what an Elo score on LMArena measures

And then our Gemini 3 model release happened in November of this year, where we were pretty happy with a lot of the benchmark results.

![Gemini 3 Pro against Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.1 across the benchmark set. Slide at [0:54:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3283s).](slide-057.jpg){fig-align="center"}

But also we were happy with where it landed in one of the ways that you evaluate these models in the wild, which is you can use this setup called [LMArena](https://lmarena.ai/) where people see responses from two anonymized models and then they say which one is better, and from lots of pairwise for their particular prompt, right, like people can go say can you please help me solve this mathematical problem, or can you help me produce a recipe for my French onion soup or something.

![Gemini 3 Pro's Arena results across categories. Slide at [0:54:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3296s).](slide-058.jpg){fig-align="center"}

And then people grade A or B, which is better, *like going to the ophthalmologist*. And through a lot of those evaluations you can get a sense of the relative strength of different models, and that's where you get an [Elo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elo_rating_system) score, a little bit like a chess ranking.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** Gemini 3 Pro shipped on November 18, 2025, about three months before this February 2026 talk, so "November of this year" means the preceding November.
:::

#### Search AI Mode: the model generates the interface

So one of the things we've been working on is [search and AI mode](https://blog.google/products/search/ai-mode-search/). We actually want these models to be able to produce the UI that the user will see.

![The generative-UI demo Dean fought the Wi-Fi to load. Slide at [0:56:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3366s).](slide-059.jpg){fig-align="center"}

I'm not sure this is going to work. Am I on the Wi-Fi? I might not be on the Wi-Fi. This is going to make me sad. All right, let's enable the hotspot. That's probably easier than logging into. One moment. Sorry. Okay. Come on. Oh, there we go. Okay, great. Go there. Go there. Yay. Thank you, T-Mobile. Okay. [laughter]

![The demo running: a research page on RNA transcription alongside AI Mode. Slide at [0:56:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3404s).](slide-063.jpg){fig-align="center"}

![The query typed into AI Mode: "show me how rna polymerase works, what are the stages of". Slide at [0:56:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3411s).](slide-064.jpg){fig-align="center"}

All right. So this is basically they put in a sort of researchy textbooky thing about some biological thing, and now they said show me how this works. And what it's done is created an interactive visualization of the material there, and you can use sliders to control the visualization and get a sense of the topics you're trying to learn about, which is pretty nice. You can see how this would be really useful for educational things.

![What the model generated in response, an interactive visualization with its own controls. Slide at [0:57:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3423s).](slide-065.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Handwritten recipe cards to a bilingual website

Here's another example. What this couple has is a bunch of recipes in English and Korean in handwritten pieces of their. Oh, I will actually since we have closed.

And so they basically are taking things like that. They're asking Gemini to take all those recipes and say translate and transcribe them in English and Korean. And then it has, any Korean speakers can maybe validate the English translation. Okay, so now they're going to say, "Please create me a bilingual website using these recipes." Okay, so there we go. And then we added some automatically generated images, and this is a website that was created from that.

![The handwritten Korean and English recipes, turned into a bilingual website. Slide at [0:58:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3509s).](slide-066.jpg){fig-align="center"}

So I think one of the things about this is that this kind of sophisticated model will enable a lot of people who maybe don't have the skills to write software to get things that they want in software form. So *I think we're going to have a lot more software in the world than we have now*. Just kind of a cute example, but I think it's good to pay attention to what these models can do and the sophistication level of the coding and problem solving they can do.

![Reactions to Gemini 3 Pro, including a 3D LEGO editor built in one shot. Slide at [0:58:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3530s).](slide-067.jpg){fig-align="center"}

![The Nano Banana Pro launch, built on Gemini 3. Slide at [0:58:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3534s).](slide-068.jpg){fig-align="center"}

#### Nano Banana Pro, and thinking in pixel space

I'll skip that. Generative models for images and for video have also been improving quite rapidly I would say. So we had an initial release of something called [Nano Banana](https://blog.google/technology/ai/nano-banana-pro/), and then we made a much more computationally expensive but higher quality version called Nano Banana Pro.

And so as examples of things, you can start with that blueprint and say please make a realistic 3D image from the blueprint. You can see how this would be quite useful for visualizing different architectural things. You can say please annotate the original transformer architectural diagram with the important things that happen in different parts of the diagram. You can see if you're reading a research paper, getting a visualization of that could be pretty useful.

![The original Transformer architecture diagram, annotated by the model. Slide at [0:59:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTTeXZrpMR0&t=3573s).](slide-070.jpg){fig-align="center"}

You can actually *view thinking in pixel space*. So here the input image is this sort of ball and ramp problem, and tell me which bucket the ball lands in, use images to solve it step by step. Right? So you can now actually see the model will generate a series of images of its reasoning.

So it goes from there. Step one, ball rolls there. Step two, the ball rolls on to three. And then step three, the ball rolls on to five. And then step four, it ends up in bucket B. And so you can sort of see how your own problem solving probably makes these mental images of what's going to happen. And the model is able to do that and actually render that.
